column1: # OWASP ZAP API scan (stage 11e) — per-rule dispositions. TAB-separated:
#   <rule id>
# SEPARATE FROM rules.tsv ON PURPOSE. That file dispositions findings against the EDGE — what a
# spider reaches without a credential: TLS, the redirect, headers on two 401s. This one
# dispositions findings against the ROUTES, read with a live bearer token. The two scans see
# different responses from the same deployment, so a rule can legitimately be tolerable in one and
# a defect in the other; a shared file would force one answer onto both questions and hide which
# scan a line was written for.
# `zap-api-scan.py -S`, fed `docs/api/openapi.yaml`. It enumerates the nine operations from the
# CONTRACT rather than crawling for links, which is what lifts stage 11c's structural ceiling: a
# baseline spider on a bearer-token API with no hyperlinks reached `Total of 3 URLs` and visited no
# route at all.
# `-S` is safe mode: it SKIPS THE ACTIVE SCAN and reads passively. zap-api-scan.py active-scans by
# default, and this repository's rule is a baseline and never an active scan — no attack payload
# against a ledger. Losing that quietly in exchange for coverage would be a worse trade than the
# gap it closes.
# "Passive" still oversells it, so: importing the definition sends ONE REQUEST PER OPERATION, and
# three of those are writes (POST an account, PUT a deposit, PUT a withdrawal). This scan therefore
# WRITES TO THE LEDGER, using the contract's own example values rather than attack payloads. That
# is harmless against a stack the `zap` job creates and destroys in the same run, and it is why
# stage 11e runs AFTER the baseline rather than before it.
# ── THE CHECK THAT MAKES A CLEAN REPORT MEAN ANYTHING ───────────────────────────────────────────
# An inert token is invisible here: every route answers 401, the passive rules read nine error
# bodies, and the scan reports clean — which looks exactly like a clean API (AGENTS.md trap 8). Two
# gates exist for that, and both are differential rather than declarative:
#   1. The token is proven live BEFORE ZAP is handed it — the same URL requested twice, once with
#      the bearer and once without, requiring 200 and 401. Non-empty is not proof: an expired or
#      wrong-audience token 401s just as silently as no token at all.
#   2. The scan must report MORE URLs than the baseline's 3. That number is the control, measured
#      on the same run rather than assumed. A scan that enumerated nothing fails here instead of
#      passing quietly.
# ── STATUS: NO DISPOSITIONS, AND THAT IS THE RESULT RATHER THAN THE STARTING POINT ──────────────
# The scan landed report-only for exactly one run. Measured, run `31277939324`:
#   Total of 14 URLs        (the baseline reaches 3, on the same stack, in the same run)
#   FAIL-NEW: 0   WARN-NEW: 1   PASS: 118        (the baseline exercises 66)
# The single finding was `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy Header Missing or Invalid [90004]`, and it
# was FIXED rather than tolerated — the header is now set in `docker/traefik/dynamic.yml`. So this
# file carries no dispositions because there is nothing left to tolerate, not because nobody
# looked. Findings gate from the next run on.
# THE FINDING IS ALSO THE ARGUMENT FOR STAGE 11e EXISTING. Rule 90004 fires on a response a browser
# could embed; the baseline only ever reached 401s, and an error body has nothing to protect. Nine
# routes with live 200 JSON responses — account balances among them — made the rule apply at once.
# That class of finding was INVISIBLE to the edge scan, not tolerated by it.
# The red half of the gate's proof is that same run: with the header absent it reported WARN-NEW: 1
# and zap-api-scan.py exited non-zero, so with the gate in place it would have failed. One variable
# changed between it and the run that must now be green.
# IGNORE means "this does not apply to this system", never "we could not be bothered". A rule that
# genuinely applies gets fixed — headers on the terminator in docker/traefik/dynamic.yml, response
# shapes in the application — rather than a line here. The first finding this scan ever produced
# was resolved that way, which is the precedent this line is asking the next reader to follow.
# ── THE SECOND ENTRY BELOW IS THIS GATE PROVING ITSELF, AND IT IS WORTH READING AS THAT ─────────
# It arrived RED, on the run that fixed a real defect. HSTS had been recorded in five documents as
# deliberately not sent while the APPLICATION sent it — the claim was written against Traefik, where
# it truly was never configured, and nobody checked the origin. When `SecurityConfig#hstsOff()`
# finally made the documents true, this scan immediately reported the header missing on all NINE
# routes and failed the job.
# That is the differential the unit test cannot give: `SecurityConfigTest` proves one chain's
# response in isolation, while this reports the DEPLOYED stack, through the proxy, on every route.
# The same scan reported `PASS: Strict-Transport-Security Header [10035]` before the fix and
# `WARN-NEW: … x 9` after it. One variable changed.
# A scanner that goes red the moment a control changes is the only kind worth having.

column3: Strict-Transport-Security Header Not Set, on all nine contract routes. The header is deliberately not sent, and unlike this file's other entries that is now ENFORCED rather than asserted: SecurityConfig#hstsOff() disables it on all three filter chains and SecurityConfigTest#hstsIsNotSentOnASecureRequest fails if it comes back (red proof measured: "Response should not contain header Strict-Transport-Security"). The reason is unchanged and is the same one .zap/rules.tsv carries: the app router is a catch-all, so a browser dialling https://localhost receives a pin on the BARE HOST, and HSTS is host-scoped and PORT-INDEPENDENT -- a one-year pin there force-upgrades http://localhost:3000 and every other local development server on the machine, clearable only through chrome://net-internals/#hsts. This is the one entry in this file that tolerates a genuine weakness rather than a non-applicable rule. A REAL DEPLOYMENT ON A REAL DOMAIN MUST SEND IT, from its own terminator, with the hostname it actually serves -- and this line must not travel with it.
